title: Postoperative pain management and opioid safety

header.contentArea: Postoperative care: analgesia and opioid safety
guidelineVersions: Faculty of Pain Medicine/RCoA/CPOC, Surgery and Opioids: Best Practice Guidelines (March 2021)
CPOC position statement on modified-release opioids (31 May 2023)

brief.scenario: Mr Aaron Dunsford, 58, has severe postoperative pain despite regular non-opioid analgesia and has become drowsy after opioid doses.
brief.task: Assess his pain and the safety of his current opioid use.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Safety first (drowsiness after opioids), then find the cause of the pain, then treat it appropriately.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Giving more opioid because he's in pain without checking sedation and respiratory rate first.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Before anything else I'd check his airway, breathing, oxygen saturation and level of consciousness."

flow: ABCDE with focus on sedation and respiratory rate
Review opioid history and total dose
Reassess pain and look for a new cause

grid.label: Recognising opioid-induced ventilatory impairment
grid.fail: Treats drowsiness after opioids as simply 'tired', without assessing ABCDE.
grid.pass: Assesses ABCDE first because drowsiness after opioids may indicate opioid-induced ventilatory impairment; checks respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and level of consciousness.
grid.high: Explains that oxygen saturation can look reassuring while hypoventilation and rising carbon dioxide continue, so clinical respiratory assessment is still needed.

grid.label: Reviewing opioid and other CNS depressant use
grid.fail: Does not establish what opioid, route, dose or timing has been given, or ignores other sedatives.
grid.pass: Reviews opioid type, route, timing and total recent dose, plus sedatives and other CNS depressants.
grid.high: Also asks about chronic opioid use and tolerance, since this changes the risk and the expected response.

grid.label: Reassessing pain and looking for a new cause
grid.fail: Assumes the severe pain is simply expected after this operation and treats it as such.
grid.pass: Reassesses pain (severity, function, likely cause) and actively looks for a new surgical complication rather than assuming pain is expected.
grid.high: Names specific complications to exclude, such as bleeding, sepsis or compartment syndrome, rather than a generic 'rule out complications'.

grid.label: Choosing safe analgesia
grid.fail: Uses a modified-release opioid routinely for acute pain in an opioid-naive patient, or simply increases the opioid dose without addressing safety.
grid.pass: Uses multimodal analgesia where appropriate; prefers oral immediate-release opioids when an oral opioid is needed, titrated to functional recovery.
grid.high: Explicitly avoids unnecessary modified-release opioids in this opioid-naive patient and explains why immediate-release is preferred for acute, self-limiting postoperative pain.

grid.label: Managing suspected opioid toxicity
grid.fail: Treats a normal oxygen saturation as proof that ventilation is safe.
grid.pass: Recognises that oxygen can mask hypoventilation and that clinical respiratory assessment (rate, depth, consciousness) is what confirms safety.
grid.high: If ventilatory impairment is significant, follows the local emergency protocol and reverses appropriately rather than simply observing.

grid.label: Escalation and stewardship
grid.fail: Manages complex or severe pain alone with no escalation and no plan beyond the ward round.
grid.pass: Escalates to the anaesthetic or acute pain team when pain is severe, complex, or opioid toxicity is suspected.
grid.high: Plans discharge opioid stewardship and patient education as part of the same review, not as an afterthought.

fail.text: He's in pain, so I'd just give him more opioid.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: His oxygen saturation is 97% on air.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That's fine then, his breathing must be safe.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What has he actually had, and when?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'm not sure, I'd just chart the next dose on time.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's expected after this operation, nothing more to check.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, I'll manage it myself on the ward.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: ABCDE first, because drowsiness after opioids can mean opioid-induced ventilatory impairment — I'd check his respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and conscious level.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: His opioid type, route, timing and total recent dose, and any other sedating drugs.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What are the opioid safety issues here?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A normal oxygen saturation doesn't guarantee safe ventilation — oxygen can mask hypoventilation, so I'd assess him clinically as well.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Is the severe pain itself a concern?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes — I wouldn't just assume it's expected. I'd reassess it and look for a new surgical complication.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you treat the pain safely?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Multimodal analgesia, and if an oral opioid is still needed I'd use an immediate-release one titrated to his function, not a modified-release opioid.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes, to the acute pain or anaesthetic team, given the severity and the toxicity concern.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: ABCDE first — drowsiness after opioids needs checking as possible ventilatory impairment, and I wouldn't be reassured by a normal saturation alone, since oxygen can mask hypoventilation while carbon dioxide rises.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What's your review of his opioids?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Type, route, timing and total dose, plus other CNS depressants, and whether he's opioid-naive or has any tolerance from chronic use — that changes how I'd interpret this.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Is the pain itself just expected?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I wouldn't assume that — I'd specifically look for bleeding, sepsis or compartment syndrome before accepting 'expected postoperative pain' as the explanation.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How would you treat him safely?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Multimodal analgesia, immediate-release opioid titrated to function if still needed, and I'd specifically avoid a modified-release opioid in an opioid-naive patient — it adds risk without benefit for acute, self-limiting pain.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Escalate to the acute pain team now given the severity and toxicity signs, and build in opioid stewardship and patient education for discharge rather than leaving that until later.

failures.move: Giving more opioid for reported pain without checking sedation or respiratory rate.
failures.consequence: Worsening opioid-induced ventilatory impairment is missed.

failures.move: Treating a normal oxygen saturation as proof that ventilation is safe.
failures.consequence: Hypoventilation and rising carbon dioxide continue undetected.

failures.move: Assuming severe pain is simply expected after surgery.
failures.consequence: A new complication such as bleeding or sepsis is missed.

failures.move: Using a modified-release opioid routinely in an opioid-naive patient.
failures.consequence: Added toxicity risk with no benefit for acute, self-limiting pain.

failures.move: Managing severe or complex pain alone with no escalation.
failures.consequence: Delayed specialist input for a patient who may need it.

recovery.when: Pushed that saturation is normal so it's safe
recovery.line: That wouldn't exclude opioid toxicity, because oxygen can mask hypoventilation — I'd still assess him clinically.

recovery.when: Asked why you won't just give more opioid
recovery.line: I'd still want to check for a new complication and confirm it's safe to give more before increasing the dose.

knowledge.fact: Drowsiness after opioids needs ABCDE assessment before treating it as 'expected tiredness'.
Oxygen saturation can be falsely reassuring in opioid-induced hypoventilation; assess clinically.
Immediate-release opioids, titrated to function, are preferred over modified-release for acute postoperative pain in opioid-naive patients.
Opioid stewardship continues from perioperative assessment through to discharge.
In a patient on therapeutic opioids, naloxone is titrated in small boluses rather than given at the full overdose dose, to avoid precipitating severe pain or withdrawal.

recall.think: Opioid-induced ventilatory impairment behind a normal-looking oxygen saturation.
recall.say: "I'd assess ABCDE first, because drowsiness after opioids may be ventilatory impairment, not just tiredness."
do: ABCDE: respiratory rate, saturation, conscious level
Review opioid dose/route/timing and other CNS depressants
Reassess pain for a new surgical cause

numbers.meaning: Naloxone starting dose for a patient on therapeutic opioids (not the larger overdose dose)

recall.trap: A reassuring oxygen saturation taken as proof that ventilation is safe.
recall.finish: Multimodal, immediate-release analgesia with escalation to the acute pain team if severe, complex, or toxicity is suspected.

sources.name: NICE NG180: Perioperative care in adults
sources.supports: Oral immediate-release opioids may be offered when postoperative pain is expected to be moderate to severe; dosing should support functional recovery

sources.name: Faculty of Pain Medicine, Royal College of Anaesthetists, Centre for Perioperative Care et al. Surgery and Opioids: Best Practice Guidelines
sources.supports: Opioid stewardship should continue from perioperative assessment through to discharge

sources.name: Centre for Perioperative Care, position statement on Modified Release Opioids
sources.supports: Modified-release opioids confer no benefit and carry increased risk compared with immediate-release for postoperative pain in opioid-naive patients; avoid modified-release opioids perioperatively

sources.name: NHS England Patient Safety Alert: risk of death from inappropriate doses of naloxone
sources.supports: In patients on therapeutic/chronic opioids, naloxone 100-200 micrograms IV titrated (not the 400 microgram-2 mg overdose dose) to avoid precipitating severe pain, withdrawal or arrhythmia

partner.opening: "He's had severe pain despite regular non-opioid analgesia and is drowsy after his opioid doses. How would you manage him?"

reveals.finding: Respiratory rate 9/min, oxygen saturation 97% on air, rousable but drowsy.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the opioid chart
reveals.finding: He has had three doses of oral morphine in the last four hours, and has also been given a sedating antiemetic.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the surgical site
reveals.finding: The wound looks normal; abdomen soft, no new tenderness.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about baseline opioid use

push.question: His saturation is 97%. Is he safe?
push.expect: Not necessarily — oxygen can mask hypoventilation; assess respiratory rate and conscious level.

push.question: What would you review about his opioids?
push.expect: Type, route, timing, total dose, and other CNS depressants such as sedating antiemetics.

push.question: Would a modified-release opioid help his pain control?
push.expect: No — avoid modified-release opioids in an opioid-naive patient; use immediate-release, multimodal analgesia.

push.question: Would you manage this alone?
push.expect: No — escalate to the acute pain or anaesthetic team given the severity and toxicity concern.

curveballs.prompt: "His oxygen saturation is fine, so he can't be opioid toxic."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Oxygen can mask hypoventilation; assess respiratory rate, depth and conscious level directly.

curveballs.prompt: "Just give him more oral morphine, that's what he's written up for."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not before reassessing sedation and respiratory rate and confirming it is safe to give more.

curveballs.prompt: "He's opioid-naive — would a modified-release tablet make sense here?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: No; modified-release opioids carry more risk with no benefit for acute pain in opioid-naive patients.
